chapter.name: Climates of India
chapter.blurb: Weather, seasons and climate, India's climate types, the factors and the monsoon, climate-related disasters and climate change.

scope_out.item: Detailed tropics and parallels of latitude
Full science of heating and cooling of land and sea

concepts.name: Weather, seasons and climate
concepts.description: The difference between weather and climate, the cycle of seasons and the six ritus of India.
concepts.idea: Weather changes daily, seasons recur every year and climate is the long-term pattern of weather.
concepts.rule: Weather is what we experience every hour or day. Climate is the pattern of weather in a region over several decades at least. Seasons occur as the Earth revolves around the Sun and recur every year. India has a rainy season or monsoon along with the usual four, and traditionally has six ritus: vasanta, grishma, varsha, sharad, hemanta and shishir.
concepts.example: Vasanta Panchami and Sharad Purnima are festivals linked to ritus.

questions.a: Weather changes with the day and season, while climate is the long-term pattern; the daily variations are part of the pattern over decades.

questions.a: Weather covers hours or days, seasons recur every year and last a few months, and climate covers several decades.

questions.a: Life, farming and food follow the seasons, so festivals such as Vasanta Panchami and Sharad Purnima mark the turn of the ritus.

questions.a: No. Today's heat is weather; climate is the long-term pattern over decades.

concepts.name: Types of climates in India
concepts.description: Alpine, temperate, subtropical, arid, tropical wet, semi-arid and tropical climates across India.
concepts.idea: India's climates range from alpine in the Himalayas to arid in the Thar.
concepts.rule: The Himalayas have an alpine climate with cold snowy winters and cool summers. Lower hills have a temperate climate with moderate winters and not-too-hot summers, where hill stations lie. The northern plains are subtropical with very hot summers, cold winters and most of the wheat. The Thar has an arid climate. The western coast has a tropical wet climate with rice and spices. The Deccan Plateau is semi-arid. Eastern India and the southern peninsula have a tropical climate with wet and dry periods controlled by monsoon winds.
concepts.example: Wheat grows mostly in the subtropical northern plains.

concepts.name: Factors of climate: latitude, altitude and the sea
concepts.description: How latitude, altitude and proximity to the sea determine climate.
concepts.idea: Places near the Equator, at low heights and near seas differ in temperature from those far from them.
concepts.rule: Near the Equator the Sun's rays are nearly perpendicular, so energy is focused on a small area and it is warm; near the poles rays are oblique and spread out. Temperature falls with altitude because air is thinner and farther from the heated surface. The sea moderates temperature: Mumbai's range is about 14 degrees C while Nagpur's is about 34 degrees C.
concepts.example: Kanniyakumari is warm all year while Srinagar is cooler.

questions.a: Latitude changes temperature as you move away from the Equator because of the angle of the Sun's rays, while altitude lowers temperature because air is thinner and farther from the heated surface.

questions.a: The coastal town has a narrow temperature range because the sea moderates it, while the hill town is cooler because of higher altitude and thinner air.

concepts.name: Winds, topography and microclimates
concepts.description: How winds and topography affect climate and what a microclimate is.
concepts.idea: Winds carry heat and moisture, mountains protect or expose land, and small areas can have their own climate.
concepts.rule: Winds from the west bring dry hot air to Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh in summer, while cold winds from across the Himalayas cause cold waves in winter. Sea winds bring moisture and rain. Topography, the physical surface features of an area, matters: the Himalayas and Karakoram protect India from cold Central Asian winds, while the flat Thar is open to hot dry winds. A microclimate is a climate localised in a small area, such as an urban heat island.
concepts.example: Cities with many buildings and little vegetation trap heat and become urban heat islands.

concepts.name: The monsoons
concepts.description: How monsoon winds form, the southwest and northeast monsoon, the role of the Western Ghats and traditional knowledge.
concepts.idea: Monsoons arise because land heats and cools faster than the ocean, reversing the winds each season.
concepts.rule: The word monsoon comes from the Arabic mausim, meaning season. In summer the Asian landmass heats up, creating low pressure, so moist winds are drawn from the ocean and bring heavy rain. In winter the land cools, giving high pressure, and winds blow from land to ocean. The southwest monsoon reaches southern India in early June and covers the subcontinent by mid-July; the Western Ghats act as a barrier. The northeast monsoon brings rain to parts of east and south India. Mawsynram receives about 11,000 mm of rain a year.
concepts.example: Fishermen on the Konkan coast predict the monsoon when normally submerged fish come to the surface.

concepts.name: Climate, culture, the economy and disasters
concepts.description: How climate shapes festivals and the economy, and the disasters it can bring: cyclones, floods, landslides and forest fires.
concepts.idea: Climate shapes festivals and livelihoods and can also cause disasters that need preparation.
concepts.rule: Festivals such as Baisakhi, Onam and Pongal link to seasons and farming. A monsoon failure hurts farming, raises food prices and forces migration. Cyclones form when intense low pressure over the sea draws in moist winds; the cloudless centre is the eye. Floods happen when water overflows onto dry land. A glacial burst occurred in Uttarakhand in 2013. Landslides are the sudden collapse of rock, soil or debris. Forest fires are uncontrolled fires. The NDRF rescues people.
concepts.example: The 2013 Kedarnath disaster followed days of heavy rain and a glacial burst.

concepts.name: Climate change
concepts.description: What climate change is, its causes, the greenhouse effect and mitigation.
concepts.idea: Human burning of fossil fuels adds greenhouse gases that trap extra heat and change climate.
concepts.rule: Climate change is a significant long-term change in the climate. Since the 19th century it has been largely driven by burning fossil fuels, deforestation and wasteful consumption. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide trap heat; this natural effect warms Earth to support life, but human activities released huge amounts in a few centuries. In early 2025 India's average temperature was 1 to 3 degrees C above normal. Mitigation includes cutting emissions, planting trees and boosting renewable energy.
concepts.example: A warmer early 2025 winter in India was shorter and milder than usual.

questions.q: List three actions an individual, a community and the government can take against climate change.
questions.a: An individual can save energy, a community can plant trees or share resources, and the government can promote renewable energy and improve efficiency.

questions.q: Why is the burning of fossil fuels linked to climate change?
questions.a: It releases greenhouse gases that trap extra heat
o: It releases greenhouse gases that trap extra heat
It cools the atmosphere by removing the heat
It removes clouds from the sky and so warms it
It creates rain that cools the ground

questions.q: Distinguish between the natural greenhouse effect and climate change caused by humans.
questions.a: The natural effect warms Earth enough to support life, whereas human emissions have added huge amounts of gases quickly, trapping extra heat and causing rapid warming.

questions.q: Explain how climate change, disasters and everyday life are linked.
questions.a: A warmer planet makes extreme events such as floods and cyclones more likely, which damage farming and property and disturb livelihoods, so preparing needs both adaptation and cutting causes.

questions.q: 'Climate change is only a problem of rich countries.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. It affects everyone, including India, where rising temperatures and disasters are already visible, so all must act.

questions.q: Create a pledge with three promises to reduce your carbon footprint at school.
questions.a: Promises such as switching off lights, using less plastic and planting a tree.
